title: Flatten 2D Vector
statement:
Build an iterator class `Vector2D` over a two-dimensional integer array `vec`. It hands out the numbers one at a time in reading order: all of row 0 from left to right, then all of row 1, and so on. Any row, or `vec` itself, may be empty.

- `Vector2D(vec)` prepares the iterator over `vec`.
- `next()` returns the next number in that order and moves past it. It is only ever called when at least one number is left.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` if some number has not been handed out yet, and `false` otherwise. It does not move the iterator.
constraints: At most 10^5 calls are made to next and hasNext
Every call to next has a number left to return
notes:
## Intuition

The simplest iterator copies every number into one flat list in the constructor and then walks an index along it. That works, but it copies the whole input before the first call. Instead, keep two pointers into `vec` itself: `row` and `col`. The only awkward part is that the next number may be several rows away when rows are empty or a row has just been used up, so both methods first slide the pointers forward to a real number.

## Approach

1. Store `vec` and start with `row = 0`, `col = 0`.
2. `skipEmpty`: while `row` is still inside `vec` and `col` has reached the end of the current row, move to the start of the next row.
3. `next`: call `skipEmpty`, read `vec[row][col]`, step `col` forward, and return the number.
4. `hasNext`: call `skipEmpty`; a number is left exactly when `row` is still inside `vec`.

## Example 1, step by step

`vec = [[1, 2], [3], [4]]`.

- `next`: the pointers are at (0, 0), so it returns `1` and `col` becomes 1.
- `next`: returns `2`; `col` becomes 2, the end of row 0.
- `next`: `skipEmpty` moves to (1, 0), which holds `3`.
- `hasNext`: row 1 is used up, so the pointers move to (2, 0); `row` is inside `vec`, so `true`. Asking again changes nothing: `true`.
- `next`: returns `4`.
- `hasNext`: the pointers move past the last row (`row = 3`), so `false`.

Output: `[null, 1, 2, 3, true, true, 4, false]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) amortized per call: each row is skipped at most once over the iterator's whole life, so all calls together cost O(rows + calls).
- Space: O(1) besides the stored reference to `vec` (the flat-copy version needs O(total numbers)).

## Pitfalls

- Several empty rows in a row: skip with a `while` loop, not a single `if`.
- `hasNext` must not consume a number; it may only move the pointers past empty space.
- An empty `vec` (no rows at all) must give `false` without reading `vec[0]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vec` | the array being iterated |
| `row` | index of the row that holds the next number (or `vec.length` when done) |
| `col` | index of the next number inside that row |
| `value` | the number `next` hands out |
